slides.lead: "Baby talk" survived the biggest stress test in infant research.
slides.sub: 67 labs on four continents ran the same experiment on 2,329 babies. Here is what held, and what shrank.

slides.head: The setup
slides.body:
Every lab used identical audio: mothers recorded talking to their own infant, and the same mothers talking to an adult.

Trials alternated, and each lab timed how long the baby kept listening to each kind.

slides.head: The effect held, at half the size
slides.body: Babies listened longer to infant-directed speech. Reliable, and about half the size the field had reported. Stronger in older babies, and when the accent matched the baby's own.

slides.head: The catch
slides.body:
The measure has almost no test-retest reliability (r = 0.09), so this is a group finding, not a test you can run on your own child.

A follow-up found no link between a baby's preference and their vocabulary at 18 or 24 months.

slides.head: What to take from it
slides.body:
Infant-directed speech is higher pitch, wider pitch swings, shorter phrases. If you have ever talked to a baby, you already do all three.

The takeaway is not "do baby talk or else". It is that a field willing to re-test its own classics at this scale is worth listening to.
